---
title: "Transforming a response"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The Provo regression response is a mean of log first fixation durations, and its predictor is [modeled cloze surprisal](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data), the negative base 2 logarithm of a fitted cloze probability. A **response transformation** changes the scale on which the model treats effects as additive. For a positive duration $T$, the course transformation is stated below.

An [expected value](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd) and a [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) change when the response is transformed; neither can generally be recovered by simply exponentiating its counterpart on the log scale. We use **residual** provisionally for the observed transformed response minus its fitted value. The later discussion of [residuals](residuals.qmd) derives its regression properties.

Logging each positive fixation before aggregation targets a mean log duration. Exponentiating it gives a **geometric mean**: for $n$ positive values, the $n$th root of their product. The fit and back transformation below keep that estimand distinct from an arithmetic mean duration, which adds the values and divides by $n$.

Why might we want a logarithm here? On the millisecond scale, equal differences receive equal size. On the log millisecond scale, equal ratios receive equal size because $\log(at)-\log(t)=\log a$. Thus the transformation determines which comparisons the regression treats as having the same size.

$$
Y=\log T
$$

turns a multiplicative change in milliseconds into an additive change on the log scale.

## What the prepared response means

For position $i$, the course table stores a mean log duration aggregated across readers, $\overline{\log T}_i$. Exponentiating it gives

$$
G_i
=
\exp\!\left(\overline{\log T}_i\right),
$$

the geometric mean duration among the retained reader measurements for that position. It does not give the arithmetic mean duration.

For two positive reader durations $t_1$ and $t_2$, the arithmetic mean is $(t_1+t_2)/2$, while exponentiating the mean log duration gives

$$
\exp\left\{\frac{\log t_1+\log t_2}{2}\right\}
=\sqrt{t_1t_2}.
$$

These summaries are equal only when $t_1=t_2$. The order of operations thus matters: taking logs before averaging targets the geometric mean after exponentiation, whereas averaging raw milliseconds and then logging targets a different summary.

```{r}
#| label: transform-provo-response
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
provo$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  provo$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
provo$ffd_geometric_mean_ms <- exp(provo$mean_log_ffd)

fit <- lm(mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c, data = provo)
residual_sd <- summary(fit)$sigma

stopifnot(
  max(abs(
    log(provo$ffd_geometric_mean_ms) - provo$mean_log_ffd
  )) < 1e-12,
  all(provo$ffd_geometric_mean_ms > 0)
)

summary(provo$ffd_geometric_mean_ms)
```

The first retained Provo position provides a data based back transformation:

```{r}
#| label: inspect-one-provo-back-transformation
provo[1L, c("position_id", "mean_log_ffd", "ffd_geometric_mean_ms")]
```

The final column is obtained by exponentiating that position's observed mean log duration. The course table does not contain the raw reader durations needed to reconstruct the corresponding arithmetic mean.

Under the working model for the stored position summaries

$$
Y_i\mid x_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu_i,\sigma^2),
$$

two summaries of the position response after returning to milliseconds differ:

$$
\operatorname{Median}(T_i\mid x_i)=\exp(\mu_i)
$$

but

$$
\mathbb{E}[T_i\mid x_i]=\exp(\mu_i+\sigma^2/2).
$$

From [expectations of functions](../random-variables-and-distributions/expectation-of-functions.qmd), the **moment generating function** of a random variable is $M_Y(t)=\mathbb{E}[e^{tY}]$. If $Y\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, that function is $M_Y(t)=\exp(\mu t+\sigma^2t^2/2)$. Setting $t=1$ gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[e^Y]=M_Y(1)=\exp(\mu+\sigma^2/2).
$$

This calculation gives the second identity above. Back-transforming a fitted log mean without the variance term thus targets a conditional median, or equivalently a geometric mean of the stored position response under this model, rather than its arithmetic mean.

The identity thus depends on the normal working model for log responses; exponentiation alone does not supply the correction.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-response-transform
#| fig-cap: "Observed geometric mean durations for each position and two summaries returned to milliseconds from the fitted model on the log scale."
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(
    min(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    max(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    length.out = 160L
  )
)
grid$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  grid$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
grid$mu <- predict(fit, newdata = grid)
grid$conditional_geometric_mean <- exp(grid$mu)
grid$working_lognormal_mean <- exp(grid$mu + residual_sd^2 / 2)

point_opacity <- 0.2
ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, ffd_geometric_mean_ms)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, conditional_geometric_mean),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, working_lognormal_mean),
    color = "black",
    linetype = 2,
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Position geometric mean FFD (ms)"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

At the observed predictor center, the fitted geometric mean is `r sprintf("%.1f", exp(coef(fit)[["(Intercept)"]]))` ms, while the working lognormal arithmetic mean of the geometric means for positions is `r sprintf("%.1f", exp(coef(fit)[["(Intercept)"]] + residual_sd^2 / 2))` ms. The small difference is computed from the actual Provo regression residual scale.

A potential worry is that this analysis diagnoses raw reader-time skew. It cannot. The prepared response has already averaged log duration by position, so the calculation demonstrates transformation and back-transformation of the stored summaries only.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Why is `exp(mean_log_ffd)` a geometric mean?
2. Which raw-scale summary includes the $\sigma^2/2$ term?
3. Does a linear effect on log duration imply a constant millisecond difference?
4. Why can this table not reveal the raw distribution across readers?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. `exp(mean_log_ffd)` equals $\exp(\overline{\log T})$, the geometric mean of the retained positive durations. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The conditional arithmetic mean under the lognormal working model is $\mathbb{E}[T\mid x]=\exp(\mu+\sigma^2/2)$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. No. A constant additive change on the log scale is a constant multiplicative ratio on the millisecond scale, so the millisecond difference depends on the baseline. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The stored response already averages log durations over readers, so individual trial values and their distribution are unavailable. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
